title: When words run out
job: Paraphrase, ask what something means, repair a misunderstanding
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Es una cosa que sirve para + V-inf
Perdona + , + no te he entendido + . + ¿Puedes repetir?

rules.text: When the thing you are describing has NOT been identified, the verb inside the relative clause goes subjunctive: busco algo que sirva, ¿hay alguien que hable español? You do not know the word, so the thing is unidentified by definition — the mood follows from the situation, not from a list.
For a thing that exists and is known, the same clause takes the indicative: tengo algo que sirve para eso. That minimal pair — sirva against sirve — is the whole rule, and it never bends.

The accidental se: se me olvidó la palabra, se me rompió el móvil. The thing becomes the grammatical subject and the person is a dative bystander — the word forgot itself to me. It is not an evasion of blame, it is the ordinary way Spanish reports an accident.

This is a THIRD se, and it is not the other two. L3-M8's passive se (se firma aquí) and L4-M7's impersonal se (se dice que) both hide the doer. This one names the person, in the dative slot: se ME olvidó, se TE rompió.

The circumlocution frames are the point of the module: es una cosa que, sirve para, es como un, parecido a, no me sale la palabra. Put an ordinary noun inside a frame and two thousand words become an unlimited vocabulary.

The repair set works in both addresses and differs only in a verb ending: ¿puedes repetir? to a friend, ¿puede repetir? to a stranger. Perdona, no te he entendido; ¿cómo se dice?; ¿qué quiere decir?; más despacio, por favor.

English marks nothing at all here. I need someone who speaks English is the same shape whoever it is, so nothing warns you that a choice is due, and alguien que habla slips out and the distinction is silently lost.

English says I lost my ticket and puts the speaker in the subject slot. Perdí el billete is correct Spanish and sounds like a confession; se me perdió el billete is the default and sounds like an accident. And English sorry does three jobs Spanish splits between lo siento, perdona and ¿cómo?

sentences.display: Es una cosa que sirve para abrir botellas. No me sale la palabra.
sentences.cue: It is a thing you use for opening bottles. The word will not come to me.
sentences.literal: Is a thing that serves for to-open bottles. Not me comes-out the word.

words.cue: a thing that, a thingy for
words.note: The opening frame of every paraphrase. What follows is a description, so the noun you cannot remember is never needed.
Always para plus an infinitive: sirve PARA abrir. Naming the job is the fastest way to describe a thing.

words.cue: it will not come to me
words.note: Said about a word you know and cannot reach. It buys you a few seconds and tells the listener you have not finished.
Feminine: la palabra. Una palabra is one word; unas palabras, from L4, is a short speech.

sentences.trap: You already know how to do this in your own language. The only thing missing is the frames, and there are four of them — that sentence is the most useful thing in this module.
sentences.sound: Cosa is KO-sa, and the s is always the sharp English s of see, never the z of rose.

variations.display: Es una cosa que sirve para abrir botellas.
variations.cue: It is a thing you use for opening bottles.
variations.changed: The frame alone. Complete, and enough to get you the word from anyone listening.

variations.cue: The word will not come to me.
variations.changed: The stall on its own, which is what you say while you build the description.

mistake.display: Es una cosa que sirve abrir botellas.
mistake.why: sirve needs its para before the infinitive. Without it the sentence has two verbs and nothing joining them.

sentences.usage: Neutral, and usable with anyone. Nobody minds a description; what strands a conversation is stopping.
sentences.mnemonic: Describe the job, not the thing.

sentences.display: Necesito algo que sirva para esto. Busco una cosa pequeña.
sentences.cue: I need something that will do for this. I am looking for something small.
sentences.literal: I-need something that may-serve for this. I-seek a thing small.

words.note: Subjunctive because the thing has not been identified. Compare tengo algo que SIRVE, for a thing you already have.
Takes no preposition: busco algo, never busco por algo. That is the commonest error a learner brings from English.
The all-purpose noun. Feminine, and the one word that lets you talk about anything you cannot name.

sentences.trap: Necesito algo que sirve is the sentence a learner produces for years. English marks nothing here, so nothing tells you that not knowing which thing is exactly what puts the verb into the subjunctive.
sentences.sound: Sirva is SIR-ba, with the Spanish v sounding like a soft b. Sirve and sirva differ only in that last vowel, so land it clearly.

variations.cue: I need something that will do.
variations.changed: The unknown thing at its shortest, with the subjunctive doing all the work.

variations.display: Tengo algo que sirve para esto.
variations.cue: I have something that does for this.
variations.changed: Known thing, indicative. The minimal pair of the module, one letter apart.

mistake.display: Busco por algo que sirve para esto.
mistake.why: Two faults. buscar never takes por, and the thing is unidentified, so the verb must be sirva.

sentences.usage: Neutral. This is shop Spanish, hardware-store Spanish, and the sentence that gets you the thing when you cannot name it.

sentences.display: ¿Hay alguien que hable español? Es que no te he entendido bien.
sentences.cue: Is there anyone who speaks Spanish? The thing is, I did not catch what you said.
sentences.literal: Is-there someone that may-speak Spanish? Is that not you I-have understood well.

words.note: The participle of entender. No te he entendido reports one moment; no te entiendo says you still do not.

sentences.trap: ¿Hay alguien que habla español? is the version everyone builds first. You do not know whether such a person exists, so the clause is unidentified and hable is required.
sentences.sound: Entendido is en-ten-DI-do, four even syllables with the stress on the third.

variations.cue: Is there anyone who speaks Spanish?
variations.changed: The question alone, and the single most useful unidentified-antecedent sentence in the language.

variations.cue: I did not quite catch that.
variations.changed: The repair alone. Said at once, it keeps the conversation alive.

mistake.why: habla is the indicative and assumes such a person exists. The whole point of the question is that you do not know, so it is hable.

sentences.usage: Neutral, and safe with strangers. Asking for help early costs nothing; the awkwardness comes from waiting.
sentences.mnemonic: Do not know who, so subjunctive.

sentences.display: Perdona, no te he entendido. ¿Puedes repetir otra vez más despacio?
sentences.cue: Sorry, I did not catch that. Could you say it again more slowly?
sentences.literal: Forgive, not you I-have understood. Can-you to-repeat another time more slowly?

words.note: Both addresses in one row: puedes to a friend, puede to a stranger. Only the verb ending moves.
Literally another time. Softer than de nuevo in speech, and the ordinary way to ask for a repeat.
An adverb already, so there is no despacia and no despaciamente. Más despacio is what you actually ask for.

sentences.trap: English sorry does three different jobs. Spanish splits them: lo siento is regret, perdona is excuse me, and for I did not hear you the word is perdona or simply ¿cómo? Choosing wrong is a small permanent tell.
sentences.sound: Despacio is des-PA-thyo in Spain and des-PA-syo elsewhere; both are standard and neither stresses the final o.

variations.cue: Could you say it again more slowly?
variations.changed: The request at its shortest, and enough on its own.

variations.cue: Could you say it again more slowly, please?
variations.changed: The same sentence to a stranger: puede, plus por favor. Politeness lives in the frame, not in the pronoun.

mistake.display: Lo siento, no te he entendido, repite rápido.
mistake.why: lo siento apologises for something you did wrong, which this is not, and rápido asks for the opposite of what you need.

sentences.usage: Both addresses, and this sentence is said as often to a clerk as to a friend. Nobody in Spanish minds being asked to repeat.
sentences.mnemonic: Perdona for the ear, lo siento for the heart.

sentences.display: Se me olvidó la palabra. Es como un vaso, pero pequeño.
sentences.cue: The word has gone out of my head. It is like a glass, only small.
sentences.literal: Itself to-me forgot the word. Is like a glass, but small.

words.cue: I forgot, it went out of my head
words.note: La palabra is the subject here, not you: the word forgot itself to me. Change the person at me, not at the verb.
Opens a comparison when the name will not come. Follow it with any noun the listener already knows.

sentences.trap: Olvidé la palabra is correct and sounds like a confession of carelessness. Se me olvidó is the default, and it reports the same event as an accident, which is how Spanish usually frames it.
sentences.sound: Se me olvidó is said as one run, se-me-ol-bi-DO, with the stress right at the end.

variations.cue: The word has gone out of my head.
variations.changed: The accidental frame alone, which is the commonest sentence in this module.

variations.cue: Words keep going out of my head.
variations.changed: Plural subject, so the verb moves to olvidan. The me does not change, because it never marks the subject.

mistake.display: Me olvidé la palabra y se me rompió el vaso ayer.
mistake.why: The accidental frame is se me olvidó, with the thing as subject. Me olvidé needs de — me olvidé DE la palabra — and means something closer to I let it slip.

sentences.usage: Neutral, and much softer than the English equivalent. It is the polite way to say the word is gone.
sentences.mnemonic: The word forgot itself to me.

sentences.display: Se me rompió el móvil y no me acuerdo de la tienda.
sentences.cue: My phone broke and I cannot remember the shop.
sentences.literal: Itself to-me broke the mobile and not me I-remember of the shop.

words.note: Same third se as se me olvidó. Move the person at the middle word: se ME rompió, se TE rompió.
Takes de before what you have forgotten: no me acuerdo DE la tienda. Dropping the de is the usual slip.

sentences.trap: Rompí el móvil says you broke it, and a Spanish listener hears an admission. Se me rompió says it broke, and nobody is being blamed — the difference is real and it is not politeness, it is the default.
sentences.sound: Rompió opens with the strong rolled r, and the stress lands on the final syllable: rrom-PYO.

variations.cue: My phone broke.
variations.changed: The accident on its own.

variations.cue: Your phone broke.
variations.changed: The person moves at the middle word, not at the verb: se ME rompió, se TE rompió.

mistake.display: No me acuerdo la tienda y se me rompió.
mistake.why: acordarse needs its de. Without it the sentence reads as though the shop were the thing remembering.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Both halves are everyday spoken Spanish and neither is an excuse; the se frame is simply what a speaker reaches for.
sentences.mnemonic: It broke on me, not I broke it.

sentences.display: ¿Qué quiere decir esto? ¿Cómo se dice en español?
sentences.cue: What does this mean? How do you say it in Spanish?
sentences.literal: What wants to-say this? How itself says in Spanish?

words.note: Literally wants to say. It is the everyday word for mean, and it is more spoken than significa.
Impersonal se: nobody in particular says it. Follow it with en español, or point at the thing.

sentences.trap: These two questions face opposite ways. ¿Qué quiere decir? asks for the meaning of a word you have heard; ¿Cómo se dice? asks for a word you have not. Mixing them is the fastest way to confuse the person helping you.
sentences.sound: Quiere decir runs together as KYE-re-de-THIR or KYE-re-de-SIR, with no pause between the two verbs.

variations.cue: What does this mean?
variations.changed: The meaning question alone, with esto pointing at whatever you are stuck on.

variations.cue: How do you say this in Spanish?
variations.changed: The word question, aimed the other way. Both are complete sentences.

mistake.why: The two frames have been crossed. Meaning is qué quiere decir; the word for something is cómo se dice.

sentences.usage: Both addresses without changing anything, because neither question has a person in it. That is part of why they are so useful.
sentences.mnemonic: Qué for meaning, cómo for the word.

sentences.display: Eso significa que la tienda no abre hoy. Es parecido a esto.
sentences.cue: That means the shop is not open today. It is similar to this.
sentences.literal: That means that the shop not opens today. Is similar to this.

words.note: The formal twin of quiere decir. Use it for a sign or a written notice; quiere decir for anything spoken.
Agrees with the thing described: una cosa parecida A esto. The a is fixed and never becomes de.

sentences.trap: Significa and quiere decir are not interchangeable in register. A notice on a door significa something; a person talking to you quiere decir it, and using significa about speech sounds like a textbook.
sentences.sound: Significa is sig-ni-FI-ka, and the g before an n keeps its hard sound.

variations.display: Eso significa que la tienda no abre hoy.
variations.cue: That means the shop is not open today.
variations.changed: Reading a sign out loud, which is where significa belongs.

variations.display: Es una cosa parecida a esto.
variations.cue: It is something similar to this.
variations.changed: The comparison frame, with parecida agreeing with cosa.

mistake.display: Es parecido de esto y no significa nada.
mistake.why: parecido takes a, never de. Spanish fixes the preposition to the adjective and there is nothing to reason out.

sentences.usage: Neutral. significa leans written and formal; the rest of the sentence is ordinary spoken Spanish.

sentences.display: No hay palabra que signifique eso. Quiero decir, no me acuerdo.
sentences.cue: There is no word that means that. I mean, I cannot remember it.
sentences.literal: Not there-is word that may-mean that. I-want to-say, not me I-remember.

words.cue: I mean, what I mean is
words.note: Repairs your own sentence mid-flight. It buys time and signals that a better version is coming.

sentences.trap: The antecedent here does not merely go unidentified — it is denied outright. No hay palabra que exista at all, so signifique is not a choice; the indicative would claim the word is there.
sentences.sound: Signifique ends in a hard k sound written que: sig-ni-FI-ke.

variations.display: No hay palabra que signifique eso.
variations.cue: There is no word that means that.
variations.changed: The denied antecedent alone, which is the strongest case for the subjunctive.

variations.display: Hay una palabra que significa eso.
variations.cue: There is a word that means that.
variations.changed: The word exists, so the mood swings back to the indicative. One letter, and the claim reverses.

mistake.display: No hay palabra que significa eso.
mistake.why: significa asserts the word exists, and the sentence has just said it does not. A denied antecedent always takes the subjunctive.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Correcting yourself out loud is normal in Spanish and quiero decir is how it is done.

sentences.display: ¿Cómo se llama esto en español? Se me olvida siempre.
sentences.cue: What is this called in Spanish? I always forget it.
sentences.literal: How itself calls this in Spanish? Itself to-me forgets always.

words.note: The same se llama that L1-M1 used for names, now asked about a thing. Point at the object as you say it.

sentences.trap: ¿Cómo se llama? and ¿Cómo se dice? both get you a word, and they are not the same request. The first asks for the name of the object in front of you; the second asks how to express an idea.
sentences.sound: Llama is YA-ma across most of the Spanish-speaking world and SHA-ma in the River Plate. Both are standard.

variations.cue: What is this called?
variations.changed: Pointing does the rest. This is the shortest complete question in the module.

variations.cue: I always forget it.
variations.changed: The accidental frame in the present, for something that keeps happening rather than something that happened once.

mistake.display: ¿Cómo se llama esto? Siempre lo olvido a mí.
mistake.why: The accidental frame is se me olvida, with the thing as subject. Lo olvido a mí doubles the person and belongs to no construction.

sentences.usage: Both addresses. Neither question has a person in it, so a market stall and a formal office get the same sentence.
sentences.mnemonic: Se llama the thing, se dice the idea.

comprehensionPool.display: Es una cosa que sirve para comer.
comprehensionPool.cue: It is a thing you use for eating.

comprehensionPool.display: Necesito algo que sirva para esto.
comprehensionPool.cue: I need something that will do for this.
Is there anyone here who speaks Spanish?
Sorry, I did not catch that.
Could you say that again more slowly?

comprehensionPool.display: Se me olvidó la palabra otra vez.
comprehensionPool.cue: The word went out of my head again.

comprehensionPool.display: Se me rompió el móvil ayer.
No me acuerdo de la tienda.

comprehensionPool.cue: How do you say it in Spanish?

comprehensionPool.display: Es como un vaso, pero pequeño.
comprehensionPool.cue: It is like a glass, only small.
